Noted difference, not a contradiction (G5-D10): Different scope. The strategy's 'vacuum' follows from having no new ICT strategy since 2017, while the Commission rates the institutional set-up. The Commission's same paragraph also asks for attention to capacity. The dates differ by eight months.

Noted difference, not a contradiction (G5-D10): Different level. The audit finds one specific gap between the ministry and the innovation fund on AI programmes. The Commission gives a general rating of the digital policy set-up. A sector gap can coexist with a general positive rating.

Noted difference, not a contradiction (G5-D10): Different objects. ITU describes a ministers' council monitoring sectoral ICT and eGovernment projects. The audit's absent body concerns systems shared by several institutions, and elsewhere it says a council for interoperability was never formed. A tension remains on how far coordination worked in practice.

Noted difference, not a contradiction (G5-D10): Different functions. The strategy says no institution is competent for implementation or inspection. The Commission says the ministry leads on digitalisation projects, and in the same sentence says modernisation lacks clear ownership. The two descriptions are largely compatible.

Noted difference, not a contradiction (G5-D10): Different counts and dates. The Commission counts services by administrative bodies accessible on the portal in April 2022. ITU counts single sign-on e-services from an earlier snapshot. The audit series moves from 50 to 212 between August 2021 and May 2022, so the count was changing fast.

Noted difference, not a contradiction (G5-D10): Different definition and probably date. 203 allow e-application by September 2022. 95 is a strategy baseline for 2022 with no month, and a footnote on page 37 of the strategy ties the number of services to the fourth level of sophistication. The audit series gives 212 in May 2022.

Noted difference, not a contradiction (G5-D10): Definitions differ but are not fully stated. The strategy counts e-services at the fourth level of sophistication, and its footnote is an unfinished note on that level. 'Fully automated' is undefined. The 230 sits close to the audit series (224 to 234), while the 95 appears to be an earlier baseline.

Noted difference, not a contradiction (G5-D10): Counting definitions probably differ. The audit separates its 234 e-services from 162 services on external portals reached through redirects, and 277 reached through the portal. The Commission's 392 'digital services' is undefined. Its own report also gives 230 and 238, so its counting is inconsistent.

Noted difference, not a contradiction (G5-D10): Different measures. The Commission's 5% has no stated source or year. The 22% is a Balkan Barometer opinion survey in which citizens report their own use. Survey self-reporting and a population usage figure are not the same indicator.

Noted difference, not a contradiction (G5-D10): Different indicators. The 36% is the overall maturity score (EU27+ biennial average). The strategy's own formula (page 147) defines 47.4% as the mean of user centricity and key enablers only. The name 'benchmark' hides the difference.
For the same Reform Agenda target on e-services in October 2024, the Agenda gives a 2024 baseline of 264 while the Commission assessment gives a current figure of 392.
The Reform Agenda gives 264 e-services as the 2024 baseline, while the Commission report gives 124 services accessible online by September 2024.

Noted difference, not a contradiction (G5-D10): Definition probably explains it. 124 are services where applications can be submitted electronically, while 392 is a wider and undefined 'digital services' count whose sentence repeats the 2023 report. The audit's categories show that such wider counts exist. Probable, not proven.
Commission documents of June and October 2024 give 246 services available online and 124 services accessible online by September 2024.
The Commission states in 2024 that most administrative services are offered online and offline, while the State Audit Office in 2024 records 1,120 services available only in person.

North Macedonia told the 2023 screening that the platform allows access to people with disabilities, while the State Audit Office finds that visually impaired persons cannot use the portal e-services.
The Commission states in 2024 that the portal caters to people with special needs, while the State Audit Office concludes in 2024 that persons with disabilities cannot use e-services.
The Commission 2020 report says the e-appeals section was still being developed, while North Macedonia reports that e-appeals became fully operational on 1 April 2019.

Noted difference, not a contradiction (G5-D10): Different points in the process. The tool can hold referral data while the referral itself is still issued on paper. The Commission's sentence is about paper use and interoperability, the country's about what the system stores. A tension remains, and practice needs checking.

Noted difference, not a contradiction (G5-D10): As for the previous pair, but both statements are the Commission's. Storing referral data and issuing referrals on paper can both be true, particularly as the screening text describes content and not process. The later wording does not say paper was ended.
In the same screening report North Macedonia says the Central Register operates as the Point of Single Contact, while the Commission identifies the Point of Single Contact as www.uslugi.gov.mk.
